programs.title: China's rural CEO experiment: How a Dai village is reinventing itself
programs.desc: During the Dai New Year, CGTN reporter Lincoln Humphries visited Manluanzhan, a traditional Dai village near China's southwestern border in Yunnan Province. This livestream showcases how traditional Chinese culture thrives in modern consumption scenarios, and how Suzhou leverages its distinctive cultural resources to create new inbound‑tourism experiences marked by greater interactivity, immersive engagement and international appeal.

programs.title: RAZOR Conversations: El Nino and Climate
programs.desc: El Nino is one of the most powerful climate phenomena on Earth, capable of reshaping weather patterns across the globe. In this episode, Neil Cairns speaks with Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long-Range Prediction at the UK Met Office, to explore how El Nino forms, how scientists predict its development, and why it can trigger extreme weather events including droughts, floods and heatwaves. From changes in Pacific Ocean temperatures to its surprising links with global atmospheric circulation and even the Earth’s rotation, the programme reveals the complex science behind this natural climate cycle. As climate change intensifies extreme weather risks, understanding El Nino is becoming increasingly important for preparing for the challenges ahead.

programs.title: RAZOR: Predicting the Unpredictable
programs.desc: Can earthquakes ever truly be predicted? RAZOR travels across Italy, from the highly active Campi Flegrei near Naples to INGV's seismic monitoring center in Rome and a leading earthquake engineering laboratory in Pavia. We meet scientists using artificial intelligence and real time monitoring to better understand seismic activity, identify areas most at risk and improve preparedness. We also explore cutting edge engineering technologies that are helping buildings withstand powerful earthquakes, asking whether science can ever predict the unpredictable, or whether the key lies in learning how to prepare for it.

programs.title: How the SCO opens doors for young entrepreneurs
programs.desc: Expanding practical cooperation within the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is nurturing new industries and development opportunities across Central Asia. CGTN speaks with Victoria Khu, co-founder of the SCOLAR Network, and Ulan Abdurazakov, CEO of Nineninesix.ai, to discuss how SCO cooperation shapes young people's education and career paths.

programs.title: Tech It Out: Microscopy expansion helps 'blow up' tiny brain tissue
programs.desc: Microscopes reveal minuscule wonders by making things seem bigger. Though such optical instruments have kept improving in the past 400 years, there are always limitations for resolution and cost. That creates a problem in studying objects at a nanoscale, like neurons, the brain's primary functional unit. Dr. Kiryl Piatkevich, the assistant professor at Westlake University in Hangzhou, then decided to go in the opposite direction. They came up with an idea not to magnify the image of an object but to magnify the object itself, to blow it up.

programs.title: Fluorescent probes help visualize live brain cells
programs.desc: Dr Piatkevich's team successfully developed a molecule that, when electrified, can glow in different fluorescent colors. These artificial molecules through a bioengineering process are introduced into a live brain and attach themselves to neurons without doing any harm. Then whenever the neurons are actively working, they light up under the microscope. This technique is known today as the "fluorescent probe." It helps visualize brain activities, allowing scientists to understand how the brain reacts when it is engaged in a specific behavior – in a much more economical and straightforward way.

programs.title: Scientists reveal secret of fat accumulation
programs.desc: People complain about how easy it is to gain weight. But for scientists, fat accumulation is a complicated process, involving nearly all tissues and organs in the body. What forms the love handles people want to get rid of so much is technically called fat tissue, which houses millions of fat cells. The fat cells are like balloons, filled with triglycerides, which gradually expand. That means obese people may have "fatter fat cells." Research has shown that the number of fat cells in both thin and obese people is more or less set during childhood. As a result, an adult has a nearly constant number of fat cells. Changes in the size of fat cells will cause the body weight to rise and fall. To work out how fat accumulates within the body, the team of Zhao Yue, a researcher from Nanjing University in China, built a high-fat diet model for mice to simulate the state of overeating in humans. They found that when too much fat flooded into the body, it didn't immediately find its way to the fat tissue, but somewhere else.

programs.title: How this gel help you stop bleeding
programs.desc: The human body will naturally form blood clots, but it can be too slow to deal with serious injuries. In fact, some injuries can kill you in just five minutes. How do we stop them quickly in a way that can work with the body? Professors Ouyang Hongwei and Hong Yi from Zhejiang University accepted the challenge.

programs.title: Meet China: Starting Green, Reaching the Future
programs.desc: In this episode of Meet China, wind becomes more than a natural force—it powers a greener future across China and Europe. A piece of fabric reveals how Chinese innovation is reshaping global perceptions of manufacturing. Ancient ruins in central China are reimagined as immersive cultural experiences, turning heritage into living memory. And in Laos, Chinese agricultural expertise is helping farmers unlock higher yields and new opportunities. From energy and textiles to tourism and farming, this episode shows how innovation is renewing tradition and connecting futures across borders.

programs.title: China's ocean economy at a turning point
programs.desc: Since elevating the goal of becoming a "maritime power" in 2012, China has made significant progress. What are the most eye-catching achievements? As the focus shifts from speed to quality, how could China's AI and digital tech edge help reshape the country's traditional maritime sectors? And in a system where a few countries still hold technological and narrative dominance, how can China gain a greater voice in rule-setting through global cooperation? Host TU Yun joins Yan Yan, a senior research fellow with the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, Qu Qiang, a professor and fellow of the Belt and Road Research Center at Minzu University of China, and Warwick Powell, an adjunct professor at Queensland University of Technology, to navigate the opportunities, challenges, and what lies beneath the surface.

programs.title: China's Industrial Chains: Threads of Resilience
programs.desc: What is clothing made from? Not just cotton or wool. Sometimes, it starts with a single drop of oil! Follow CGTN as we reveal how a drop of crude oil transforms into our clothes, uncovering a complex and fascinating journey of the textile and garment manufacturing process. Follow CGTN's Wang Tianyu and take a closer look at China's textile and garment industry, and unravel the threads that connect China's industrial past, present and future.
